extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of Montaigne / general readers of Renaissance essays
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading of Montaigne's Essays (passages on liberality, magnificence, conquest, and greatness) to extract his evaluative judgments and examples about rulers, spectacles, and human nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: True liberality / generosity
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberality properly understood is tied to liberty and should not be exacted as a debt; gifts that create obligation produce mercenary loyalty rather than genuine friendship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording and examples: 'the overplus is called benefit, which cannot be exacted: for the very name Liberality sounds of Liberty.' Montaigne warns that princes who exhaust themselves in giving become poorer in friends because immoderate gifts increase desire and ingratitude. The Cyrus anecdote illustrates that binding people by reciprocal obligation (having them contribute) yields more faithful 'treasurers'—friends who are not mere mercenaries. Philip's advice to his son ('Do it, then, by the benefits of thy virtue, and not by those of thy chest') is offered as guidance: win affection by virtue rather than by monetary largess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnificence judged by novelty and invention, not mere expense
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacles and public magnificence are excusable where invention and novelty create wonder; expense alone does not justify such vanities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne contrasts extravagant Roman/imperial games with the value of inventive spectacle: 'If there be anything excusable in such excesses as these, it is where the novelty and invention create more wonder than the expense.' He gives examples of elaborate stage-machines, artificial seas, moving mountains, and other marvels—praising imaginative ingenuity while implicitly condemning mere costly display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about judging eras from present knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not conclude the world's decline or youth from limited contemporary evidence; human knowledge is short both in time and in scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne emphasizes the narrowness of human understanding: 'our knowledge is weak in all senses; we neither see far forward nor far backward.' He argues that what seems novel or decaying to us may simply reflect our limited perspective, and that discoveries elsewhere (e.g., Americas) show we may grossly underestimate the variety and extent of the world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess civilizations on their own merits, not by external standards
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating other peoples, recognize their arts, industries, virtues, and social arrangements rather than assuming inferiority because they differ (e.g., lack of coin or differing customs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne points out the sophistication of American civilizations (Cusco, Mexico): magnificent cities, gardens, manufactures in jewels/feathers/cotton, and moral qualities like devotion and loyalty. He notes practical differences (use of coin, hoarding of gold) that explain apparent disparities in wealth, urging judgment 'on their own terms' rather than through European assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral test of conquest: civilizing vs. corrupting
rubrics_metrics.description: Conquest should be judged by whether conquerors improved and civilised the peoples they subdued or whether they corrupted, enslaved, and plundered them for profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne contrasts an ideal conquest—'gently levelled...cherished and propagated the good seeds that nature had there produced'—with the Spanish practice of taking advantage of ignorance to introduce 'treachery, luxury, avarice' and commit massacres for 'pearl and pepper.' He argues that extending faith by force is not effective; true extension of religion or polity requires winning people, not slaughter and robbery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condemnation of treachery and cruelty as measures of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: False accusations, torture for treasure, and public executions (even of kings) are signs of barbarity and injustice that discredit the conquerors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne recounts the ransom and later false accusation, torture, and execution of the king of Peru and the torments inflicted on the king of Mexico and his nobles. He calls these acts 'horrid and unheard of barbarity' and notes that such behavior moved many to hate and disesteem the Spanish captains; the narratives serve as moral evidence against the supposed justice of the conquerors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs and burdens of greatness / rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Greatness and supreme power impose intolerable weight and difficulties; being a king is among the most painful and difficult employments, and superiority brings envy and imperfect judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne states 'The most painful and difficult employment in the world, in my opinion, is worthily to discharge the office of a king.' He notes the impossibility of keeping measure in boundless power, that small deeds are magnified and recorded, and that rulers' actions address a people 'no very exact judge, easy to deceive, and easily content.' He cites Otanes who relinquished a claim to the throne to live free of authority as an exemplar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of a moderate life and voluntary refusal of greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: Refusing greatness and living a moderate life is a plausible virtue—attainable and often preferable to the burdens of eminence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne presents personal preference for moderation: he would 'rather be the second or third in Perigord than the first at Paris.' He considers avoiding the climb above one's birth fortune as deliberate and virtuous, arguing that moderation aligns desires to capacity and spares one the oppressions of supreme reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rank undermines genuine competition and the ruler's share in contests
rubrics_metrics.description: Those of high rank are deprived of true contests of honour because others hold back, refuse sincere rivalry, or conspire to protect a prince's dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne observes that 'by force of respect itself men use princes disdainfully and injuriously'—participants in contests will not exert full effort against a prince, thereby denying him true participation in the trial. This phenomenon makes public displays of virtue or skill less authentic for those elevated above others.
